name: James Turrell
bio: James Turrell (born 1943) studied perceptual psychology at Pomona College before turning to art in Los Angeles, where he became a central figure in the Light and Space movement. His first works, from 1966, were projection pieces in which a beam of light seems to become a solid shape in the corner of a dark room. He went on to make Skyspaces, chambers with an opening in the roof that frame the sky as a flat field of colour, Ganzfelds that dissolve all sense of depth, and works that use the architecture of whole buildings. Since 1979 he has been transforming Roden Crater, an extinct volcano in Arizona, into a naked-eye observatory. Aten Reign (2013) filled the rotunda of the Guggenheim with changing coloured light. He received the National Medal of Arts in 2013.
studyNotes: Light is the material, perception is the subject. There is often no object at all; what you see is your own eye adjusting.
Frame the sky. A Skyspace is an aperture with a carefully shaped edge, so the sky reads as a painted surface on the ceiling. Watch how dusk changes it.
Time is part of the work. Many pieces need several minutes of looking before they change; the duration is designed.
Architecture as instrument. Rooms are built to remove edges, shadows and reference points, and that precise construction is what makes the light seem to float.
